Definition: A formal process for proposing, approving, scheduling, implementing, and reviewing modifications to production systems.
The group that reviews, approves, defers, or rejects proposed non-standard changes to production systems.
Keeping systems in a known, approved state (a baseline) and detecting configuration drift away from it.
Configuration Management Database -- the system of record for assets (configuration items) and their relationships, on which every other control depends.
Procurement, operation, maintenance, and decommissioning of assets, recorded against the CMDB.
Endpoint Detection and Response -- a behavior-based endpoint platform combining a lightweight agent, cloud analytics, and active response.
Extended Detection and Response -- EDR extended with network, identity, email, and cloud telemetry for cross-domain detection.
Host-based Intrusion Detection / Prevention Systems -- file-integrity monitoring, log analysis, and blocking on a single host; older terminology whose functions EDR platforms now include.
A per-host packet filter, critical for limiting lateral movement.
Endpoint Privilege Management -- removes local administrator rights and elevates approved applications on demand.
Allowing only approved executables to run (App Control for Business, formerly WDAC; AppLocker; fapolicyd).
Linux mandatory access control systems that confine processes to defined policies; SELinux runs in enforcing, permissive, or disabled mode.
Attack Surface Reduction -- removing what an attacker can reach and monitoring for new exposure; on Windows, Defender ASR rules block specific risky behaviors at the OS level.
Extraction of credentials from process memory or system stores (Mimikatz, LSASS read).
Living-off-the-Land Binaries -- built-in OS tools attackers use to avoid dropping new files (certutil, regsvr32, mshta, PowerShell).
Running malicious code inside the memory of a legitimate process to borrow its privileges and trusted name (MITRE ATT&CK T1055).
Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver -- loading a signed but buggy driver to disable kernel-level security agents.
Remote rendering of web content so that renderer compromises cannot reach the user's endpoint.
Network Intrusion Detection (out-of-band, alerts) / Prevention (inline, can block) Systems that run rule-based and behavioral analysis at chokepoints.
Outbound and return traffic taking different paths, which commonly breaks stateful firewalls.
An attack exploiting trunk-port misconfiguration to reach segments that should be unreachable.
Adjusting the TCP maximum segment size option to avoid fragmentation across VPN tunnels with smaller MTU.
Routing protocols or configurations that accept unauthenticated or unvalidated updates, enabling route injection and hijacking (for example, BGP without prefix filtering or RPKI).
Per-workload network policy enforced at the host or hypervisor.
Injecting a forged answer into a resolver's cache so users are sent to attacker-chosen addresses.
Cryptographic signing of DNS records to prevent forgery.
Defensive DNS responses that redirect queries for known-bad domains to controlled addresses.
Bulk DNS zone replication, which must be restricted so internal naming maps do not leak.
DNS over HTTPS / DNS over TLS -- protocols that encrypt DNS resolution traffic.
Sender Policy Framework -- a DNS record listing IPs authorized to send email for a domain (checked against the envelope sender).
DomainKeys Identified Mail -- a cryptographic signature over email headers and body verified via a DNS-published public key.
A policy framework requiring an aligned SPF or DKIM pass for the visible From domain and instructing receivers how to handle failures (none, quarantine, reject).
Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions -- certificate-based signing and encryption of individual email messages between specific senders and recipients.
Distributed Denial of Service -- attacks in three categories (volumetric, protocol, application), each requiring different mitigations.
Mobile Device Management / Unified Endpoint Management -- the centralized control plane for enrolled mobile and desktop devices.
Removal of corporate container contents on a BYOD device without touching personal data.
Sandboxing work data on personal devices (Android Enterprise work profile, Apple User Enrollment, Intune App Protection).
Corporate-Owned Business-Only / Corporate-Owned Personally Enabled / Bring Your Own Device -- three deployment models with distinct security implications.
